issues.explanation: 'Noticing Weapons' is a poor fit for the stated trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is evidence of weapon-related assault or generalized violence cues; the rest of the profile centers on interpersonal abuse and nonspecific danger rather than weapon-focused threat monitoring, so this item is hard to reconcile with the trauma context.

'Inaction Guilt' is clinically questionable in this context because it implies self-blame for not doing more to stop the abuse, which is less coherent with an ongoing coercive partner-abuse formulation than appraisals centered on shame, powerlessness, betrayal, or worthlessness. It is not impossible, but paired with the rest of the profile it stands out as weakly aligned with the trauma narrative and node pattern.

vignette:
Bao, a meticulous 51-year-old tax inspector, presented as a man holding himself together with immense effort. For months, his world had been shrinking, a process so gradual he had almost convinced himself it was a normal part of aging. The story of how his life had become so small began three years prior, in the final, violent months of a relationship that had ended abruptly. He spoke of his former partner with a detached precision, as if auditing a failed business rather than recounting a personal history. The abuse had been erratic, often exploding without warning. Bao recalled that the worst incidents happened when he was exhausted, late at night after long days at work, when his physical and mental defenses were at their lowest. It was this unpredictability, this sense of being ambushed when he was most vulnerable, that seemed to have left the deepest scars.

Now, fragments of those nights tear through his carefully ordered present. While reviewing a complex corporate tax return, the image of a hand gripping his arm will flash behind his eyes, vivid and unsolicited, only to vanish a second later. He described these moments as an unwanted intrusion, a memory that forces its way into his mind no matter how hard he tries to focus on the tax code. Other times, he finds himself trying to reconstruct the sequence of a particular evening, only to hit a wall of absolute blackness. These memory gaps are profoundly unsettling for a man who prides himself on detail and recall; it feels like parts of his own history have been stolen from him.

His sense of safety has been completely eroded. At work, Bao can no longer sit in the large, open-plan office without feeling a prickling dread. He has started taking his lunch at his desk and will only agree to meetings in conference rooms where he can secure the chair in the corner, his back pressed firmly against the wall. From there, he can see the door and everyone in the room, a strategy that provides a fleeting sense of control. Walking the few blocks from the bus stop to his office has become an ordeal; he finds himself constantly checking behind him, convinced that footsteps are quickening their pace to catch up to him. He knows, logically, that these are just ordinary city sounds, but his body reacts as if danger is imminent, his heart hammering against his ribs in a series of false alarms that leave him breathless and shaky.

These feelings are most acute when he is tired. A poor night's sleep or a demanding day at the office leaves him feeling raw and exposed. On those days, any unpredictable situation-a last-minute change to his work schedule, his wife being late home from the store-can send him into a quiet panic. He retreats into himself, overwhelmed by a profound sense of physical discomfort that settles deep in his gut. It is in these moments that his darkest beliefs surface. He has come to feel that he was fundamentally broken by the betrayal of a person he once trusted completely. This sense of having been violated has curdled into a conviction that nothing good can happen to him anymore, that he is simply waiting for the next bad thing. He confided that he often feels like an object, not a person-a thing that was used and damaged, no longer fully human.

This feeling of dehumanization has created a painful distance in his marriage. His wife is kind and patient, but when she reaches for him, he often flinches. The touch feels less like an act of affection and more like a precursor to something else. He sees the hurt in her eyes but cannot explain the chasm between them. It was after one such evening, when his involuntary recoil left his wife in tears, that Bao finally made an appointment. He came to therapy not with a clear hope for recovery, but with the quiet, desperate fear that if something did not change, he would lose the one good thing he had left.
